planning_assumptions.rental_target: Professionally managed 3-bedroom townhome with a $2,600/month primary ceiling and a $2,900/month hard stretch cap (income-based; see rental_budget_config).

home_budget_model.summary: Replaces the earlier $820K placeholder with a budget derived from lending rules, mortgage-rate forecasts and each location's property tax and insurance. On the planned career path it runs ~$727K-$895K depending on the state: about where $820K sat on average, but property tax makes it lower in Texas, Ohio and New Jersey and higher in Tennessee, the Carolinas and Alabama. A few high-tax towns sit below the state figures: Alamo Heights (~2.19% effective) at ~$698K and Celina's MUD/PID neighborhoods (~2.1%) at ~$705K.
home_budget_model.method: Budget = the price whose monthly principal, interest, property tax and insurance equal 28% of gross household income in 2041, with 20% down on a 30-year fixed loan. Home prices project from 2026 at 2.5%/yr.

front_end_ratio.source: The 28/36 rule (Chase, Bankrate); matches this plan's own 28% rent rule. Lenders will approve more - Fannie Mae allows total debt-to-income to 45%, up to 50% via automated underwriting - so 28% is the disciplined budget, not the approval limit.

down_payment.source: Avoids PMI. Typical 2026 buyers put down less (first-time ~8-10%, repeat ~19%), so 20% is a savings target, not a given.

mortgage_rate.source: Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year fixed: 7.03% on Sep 24, 2026. MBA forecasts 6.5% for 2026-2028; Fannie Mae 6.5% (2026) and 6.7% (2027). 2041 rates are unknowable, so the model uses the consensus forecast and shows +/-1 point.

household_income_2041.source: $105K household in 2026 (Gregg $73K, spouse $32K) growing 3.5%/yr. Planned step-up: Product Manager at Sherwin-Williams at ~$120K by 2030 - below the ~$136K average of SW's $102K-$156K PM range. AI leader: ~$180K by 2033, the 25th percentile of U.S. Senior AI PM pay ($181,896, Glassdoor).

property_tax.source: Effective rates on owner-occupied homes. Tax Foundation 2026 state figures (TN 0.52%, TX 1.40% state, OH 1.36%, IA 1.33%, SC 0.46%, AL 0.37%, NJ 1.88%, GA/FL ~0.80%); county figures where known (Collin 1.66%, Williamson TX 1.82%, Solon 1.92%, Melissa 1.59%). Texas entries without a county figure use 1.70%, the average of the two sourced metro counties. NC, KS and VA are estimates.

insurance.source: NerdWallet 2026 state averages for $400K dwelling coverage (TX $4,915, KS $5,455, OH $3,375, GA $3,225, NC $2,540 and others); Tennessee $3,045 (MoneyGeek); Florida inland ~$3,000 from Seminole $2,090 and Orange $3,610 county averages; VA/NJ use the ~$2,490 national average.

home_budget_model.downside: Without any step-up the budget falls to ~$559K-$688K, and 36 of 51 locations would be over budget. The career step-up is the assumption the purchase phase rests on.
home_budget_model.down_payment_check: 20% down on a ~$727K-$895K home is ~$145K-$179K by 2041.
caveats: Ignores HOA fees, PMI and other monthly debts - any of these lowers the budget.
Property-tax and insurance rates are held at 2026 levels.
NC, KS and VA property-tax rates are estimates, not sourced figures.
home_budget_model.scoring_link: housing_affordability_2041 is scored on each location's planned-path headroom (budget minus projected 2041 price) using the same curve the original scores implied; the curve reproduces 36 of 51 original scores within half a point against the old $820K.

planning_assumptions.appreciation_assumption: 2–3% annual appreciation planning assumption based on the user's stated May 2026 consensus framing.
planning_assumptions.football_weighting_note: High school football culture is treated as a nice-to-have, not a hard requirement.

default.label: Baseline (remote work, current situation)
default.basis: Matches Gregg's actual situation: fully remote for Sherwin-Williams, so no location requires an employer change. Career ceiling is weighted 15 as long-horizon option value rather than 25 as an immediate constraint, with the freed points going to rental quality, AACSB/professor path and the maker/fitness community.

alternates.label: Private school scenario (income-contingent)
alternates.basis: Assumes household income supports private tuition at enrollment. Public school quality zeroed as a direct substitute. Rebased on the remote-work baseline.

alternates.label: Career-ceiling priority (in-person)
alternates.basis: The former baseline. Weights the AI/product career ceiling at 25 - the view to use if Gregg ever wants to prioritise stepping into an in-person senior/executive product role over the remote-work status quo.

criteria.label: AI / Tech Product Career Ceiling
criteria.description: Long-horizon upward-mobility ceiling: where Gregg could step up into senior or executive AI/product leadership later in the 2026-2041 window. Because he works fully remote for Sherwin-Williams, this is NOT a measure of whether he needs a local job on arrival - no candidate location requires him to change employers. Read it as career option value: depth of senior roles to move into, in-person leadership opportunities that remote work cannot reach, and fallback market strength if he ever leaves or is laid off.
criteria.scoring_note: Scores track market depth, which correlates with but is not identical to ceiling. A market can be large in junior/IC roles yet thin in senior AI product leadership. Treat a high score as 'more senior roles exist to move into', not 'easier to get hired tomorrow'.

criteria.label: Elite Public School District Fit
criteria.description: Likelihood of accessing strong public school zones, generally targeting 7/10+ GreatSchools or equivalent quality indicators.

criteria.label: Home Purchase Affordability by 2041
criteria.description: Fit against each location's 2041 home budget from planning_assumptions.home_budget_model: the price whose principal, interest, property tax and insurance equal 28% of planned-path household income, with 20% down at 6.5%. Scored on headroom between that budget and the 2026 median projected at 2.5%/yr.

criteria.label: 2028 Rental Feasibility
criteria.description: Likelihood of finding professionally managed 3-bedroom townhome rentals near target schools and lifestyle nodes around or near the ~$2,200/month planning target.

criteria.label: State Income Tax Burden
criteria.description: Lower state income tax burden is better. No-income-tax states receive stronger scores, though property/insurance costs should be reviewed separately.

criteria.label: AACSB Density (Teaching Optionality)
criteria.description: Number of AACSB-accredited business schools within roughly a 30-40 mile drive, quality-adjusted. Measures REDUNDANCY for the eventual professor-of-practice path, not proximity to a single school: being rejected by one institution should not end the academic option. The radius reflects that this stage is unlikely to be a daily commute - adjunct and professor-of-practice roles are often 1-2 days per week or partly online.
criteria.scoring_note: 10 = 5+ AACSB institutions in radius; 9 = 4; 8-8.5 = 3; 7-7.5 = 2 with at least one strong option; 5.5-6.5 = 1-2 thin. Note ACBSP accreditation does NOT count - it is a different body. A single elite school scores lower than several solid ones, which is the point: this criterion buys optionality, not prestige.

criteria.label: Robotics, Fitness, Maker, and Indie Builder Lifestyle
criteria.description: Fit for robotics + AI interests, hardware/maker culture, fitness events such as running festivals and HYROX-style training, and indie builder/community opportunities.

criteria.label: High School Football Culture
criteria.description: Local high school football culture. This is intentionally treated as a nice-to-have lifestyle bonus, not a hard requirement.

criteria.label: Sports-Tech Venture Ecosystem
criteria.description: Viability of founding and growing a sports-technology business after leaving corporate: sports-specific engineering and R&D clusters, league/governing-body and sports-business headquarters as customers and partners, pro and major-collegiate franchises, athlete-facing training infrastructure, and vertical-relevant talent and capital.
criteria.scoring_note: Carved out of robotics_fitness_startup_fit, which now covers personal robotics/fitness fit rather than the venture dimension. Scores reward buildable ecosystem - engineering clusters and HQs you could sell into or hire from - over spectator access alone; a metro with several pro teams but no sports-tech industry scores mid, not high.

Inside a 40-mile radius there are four accredited business schools: NKU's Haile College of Business (~8 mi), the University of Cincinnati's Lindner College (~10 mi), Xavier's Williams College (~12 mi) and Miami University's Farmer School (~40 mi). If one teaching application fails there are three more without moving. Only Cary and the two Jersey City entries score higher. Career access is the Cincinnati metro: Procter & Gamble and Kroger both hiring AI engineers (P&G from $140K entry-level), Fifth Third and Western & Southern in fintech AI at $110K-$185K+, GE Aerospace, and the Cintrifuse accelerator. Average AI salary in the metro is $126,188 and the University of Cincinnati projects 34% growth in AI roles by 2031. Kentucky has cut its flat income tax to 3.5%. Football is better than the rest of the heartland set - Northern Kentucky is a real football region, with Highlands in nearby Fort Thomas among the winningest programs in the country.

key_learnings.learning: No submarket compensation premium. Compensation is set at metro level, not by suburb; higher incomes in premium suburbs (Franklin/Brentwood, Alpharetta, Frisco) reflect who lives there, not employer pay premiums. Where a metro's tech/product employers concentrate in the urban core, core-adjacent suburbs can outperform premium suburbs on career market at materially lower cost. Apply this test to any entry scored primarily on proximity to a suburban office park.

Low school-zone boundary risk is a scoring asset. Where multiple strong public zones exist (e.g. Hendersonville's three 5-star high schools), address-level zone risk is minimal, unlike single-zone-dependent markets (Georgetown TX Leander/Liberty Hill dependency). A school score backed by multiple strong zones carries less downside variance than an equivalent score in a single-zone market.

The rental phase is 13 years and covers all of K-8, while the purchased home covers only the last ~3 years of high school. School quality therefore matters more for the rental location than the purchase location. Screen any 'cheap rent now, good schools later' plan by asking which phase the child's K-8 actually falls in - and prefer locations strong on BOTH rent and schools, which need no phase split at all.

There are two employer-continuity anchors, not one, and they pull to different metros: Gregg's Sherwin-Williams tenure anchors to Cleveland (HQ), while the spouse's Kendra Scott store anchors to the Nashville metro (Franklin). Austin is the only candidate that serves both careers by upgrade rather than continuity - the strongest AI/product market for Gregg plus Kendra Scott's corporate HQ for the spouse. Any plan should state explicitly which career is being asked to restart.

Gregg works fully remote for Sherwin-Williams, so no location requires him to change jobs and the 25%-weighted ai_tech_pm_market criterion overstates its real constraint. Re-ranking under the remote scenario barely moves the order - the top five are identical - which shows the leading locations win on schools, housing and tax rather than local job market. The practical effect is on framing, not ranking: the spouse's store becomes the household's only hard geographic tie.

The AI/product career criterion was reweighted 25 -> 15 once it was clarified as long-horizon upward mobility rather than immediate employability (Gregg is fully remote). The former 25-weight baseline is retained as the 'career-ceiling priority' scenario. Notably the top of the ranking barely moved, confirming the leading locations were never winning on job market.

Added sports_tech_ecosystem (weight 5, carved from robotics_fitness_startup_fit 9->4) to capture the planned post-corporate sports-technology venture - the middle stage of a corporate -> startup -> professor arc that the model previously ignored. It rewards buildable ecosystem (engineering clusters, league and governing-body HQs) over spectator access, which is why Concord and Frisco lead while three-pro-team metros without a sports industry score mid.

The academic criterion was reframed from proximity-to-nearest to DENSITY within a 30-40 mile radius, because the real concern is optionality - being denied by one school should not end the professor path. This reversed several results. Austin has only two AACSB schools inside the radius of Round Rock (UT McCombs and St. Edward's; Texas State is ~45 mi, and Concordia and Huston-Tillotson are ACBSP not AACSB), while Cleveland has five (John Carroll, Case Western, Cleveland State, Kent State, Akron). A single elite school is worth less than several solid ones when the goal is redundancy.

Learning 3 has an inverse that the flat ranking hides. If the 13-year rental window governs schooling, then a district that is rentable but unbuyable captures nearly all the educational value while failing only the criterion that governs the final ~3 years. Lucas is the case: Lovejoy ISD is 5th of 951 Texas districts and a 3BR rents for ~$2,461 inside the $2,600 ceiling, yet a ~$1.1M median puts the 2041 purchase at roughly double budget. It scores 71.8 flat - Tier 3 - while being one of the strongest rental-phase options in the matrix. Read housing_affordability_2041 and rental_feasibility_2028 as gates on different phases, never as one blended affordability signal.

School district access is not always a function of where you buy. Lovejoy ISD - 5th of 951 in Texas - accepts out-of-district transfers for reported tuition of $8,000-$10,000/yr, roughly a third the cost of private school, which would let an elite district be bought into from a cheap housing market rather than an expensive one. This breaks the assumption running through the whole matrix that school_quality is a property of the location. Before treating any unaffordable elite district as closed, check for a transfer program, and check whether the district extends into a cheaper adjacent submarket - Lovejoy reaches Fairview, Parker, Seis Lagos and parts of Allen and McKinney, not just the $1.1M Lucas market.
key_learnings.caveat: Transfer programs are capped, annually renewed and revocable, so they are an option to price, never a plan to rely on.

key_learnings.learning: The biggest state-level cost difference for the 2041 purchase is property tax, not income tax. At the same income, a Tennessee buyer (~0.52% effective) can afford ~$895K where a Collin County buyer (1.66%) can afford ~$741K - a ~$154K gap that the income-tax criterion never captured, because Texas scores 10/10 on state_tax_burden. The old flat $820K budget hid this; the per-location budget model exposes it.

phase_plan.core_insight: The rental phase is 13 years, not 3. No children yet, but a first child born 2026-2028 would be 0-2 in 2028 and roughly 13-15 in 2041, so the rental window covers ALL of K-8 plus the start of high school, while the purchased home covers only the last ~3 years of high school. School quality therefore governs the RENTAL location more than the purchase location - the reverse of the intuitive reading. A location that is cheap to rent but weak on schools does not become safe just because the purchase is planned elsewhere.
